# Building Plots with ggplot2

This lesson teaches you how to explore a new dataset with some quick plots, and then how to make plots with ggplot2. Next week (Data Visualization II), we step back and think about the principles and practices of making *good* plots.

We start by loading the required packages. **`ggplot2`** is included in the **`tidyverse`** package.

```{r load-package, message=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

## Our data: environmental impact statements

This week we'll the full version the of the EPA's Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) data. When a federal agency wants to do something that could significantly affect the environment, like build a highway or sell timber, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) says it has to write an EIS and file it with the EPA. Each row in our data is one of those filings, from 1987 through January 2026.

The [codebook](https://ucd-rdavis.github.io/R-DAVIS/data/eis_codebook.md) describes every column. We'll call this first version `eis_raw`, since we're going to make some changes to it later on.

```{r load-data, message=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
eis_raw <- read_csv("https://ucd-rdavis.github.io/R-DAVIS/data/eis_clean.csv")
```

## Exploring the data

Whenever you get a new dataset, it's a good idea to spend some time poking around in it before you try to do anything fancy. This is called *exploratory data analysis*, and a lot of it is just making tables and quick plots to see what's in each column. You've already seen a couple of tools for this:

```{r eda-overview, purl=FALSE}
glimpse(eis_raw)
summary(eis_raw)
```

For a categorical column, one of the first things you might want to know is how many times each value shows up. The base R function `table()` does that:

```{r eda-table, purl=FALSE}
table(eis_raw$document_type)
```

That's a lot of document types! Most of them are some version of a draft or a final statement, plus a handful of short codes like `LD` and `DC`. It's easier to see what's going on if we sort the table:

```{r eda-table-sorted, purl=FALSE}
sort(table(eis_raw$document_type), decreasing = TRUE)
```

And even easier if we make it into a picture. The base R function `barplot()` takes a table and draws a bar for each value. `las = 2` turns the axis labels sideways so they fit:

```{r eda-barplot, purl=FALSE}
barplot(sort(table(eis_raw$document_type), decreasing = TRUE), las = 2)
```

It's not the prettiest plot, and some of the labels get cut off, but with one line of code we can see that almost all of the filings are plain drafts or finals.

Let's do the same thing for `epa_impact`, the EPA's rating of the environmental impact of each project. Adding `useNA = "ifany"` tells `table()` to count the `NA` values too:

```{r eda-impact, purl=FALSE}
table(eis_raw$epa_impact, useNA = "ifany")
barplot(table(eis_raw$epa_impact, useNA = "ifany"))
```

That's a lot of `NA` values. Keep that in mind, we'll come back to it next week.

For a numeric column like `filed_year`, we could also make a table:

```{r eda-year-table, purl=FALSE}
table(eis_raw$filed_year)
```

But that's a lot of numbers to read. A *histogram* shows the same information as a picture. It splits the values into bins and draws a bar for how many values fall into each bin:

```{r eda-hist, purl=FALSE}
hist(eis_raw$filed_year)
```

By default R picks the bins for you, but we can set them ourselves with the `breaks` argument. Here we make one bin for each year:

```{r eda-hist-breaks, purl=FALSE}
hist(eis_raw$filed_year, breaks = 1986:2026)
```

Now we can see that filings peaked in the mid-2000s and have mostly gone down since. The last bar is tiny because the data stop in January 2026, so we only have a few weeks of filings for that year.

## Getting the data ready to plot

Before we start plotting, we're going to make a few changes to the data. We'll do them one step at a time so we can see what each one does.

First, let's get rid of the 2026 filings, since we only have part of that year. We'll save the result as a new object called `eis`, so we still have `eis_raw` if we ever need to go back:

```{r clean-year, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis_raw %>%
  filter(filed_year <= 2025)
```

Next, let's deal with all those document types. For this lesson we mostly care whether a filing is a draft or a final statement. The function `str_detect()`, from the tidyverse package **`stringr`**, checks whether a piece of text contains a pattern and returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

```{r str-detect, purl=FALSE}
str_detect("Draft Supplement", "Draft")
str_detect("Final Supplement", "Draft")
```

We can use it inside `case_when()`, which you saw in week 5, to make a new `stage` column. Anything that doesn't contain "Draft" or "Final" (those short codes) goes into "Other":

```{r clean-stage, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis %>%
  mutate(stage = case_when(
    str_detect(document_type, "Draft") ~ "Draft",
    str_detect(document_type, "Final") ~ "Final",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  ))

table(eis$stage)
```

Now for the agencies. 92 is too many to plot, so we'll keep the six agencies with the most filings and lump everyone else into an "Other agencies" group. First we find the top six. `slice_head()` keeps the first six rows, and `pull()` pulls a column out of a dataframe as a plain vector:

```{r top-agencies, purl=FALSE}
top_agencies <- eis %>%
  count(lead_agency, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  pull(lead_agency)

top_agencies
```

Then we use `if_else()` and `%in%` to make the new column:

```{r clean-agency, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis %>%
  mutate(agency = if_else(lead_agency %in% top_agencies, lead_agency, "Other agencies"))

table(eis$agency)
```

R sorts text alphabetically, which doesn't make much sense for `epa_impact`, since the ratings go from best to worst. Turning the column into a factor lets us set the order of the categories ourselves, and ggplot will use that order when we plot:

```{r clean-impact, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis %>%
  mutate(epa_impact = factor(epa_impact, levels = c("Lack of Objections",
                                                    "Environmental Concerns",
                                                    "Environmental Objections",
                                                    "Environmentally Unsatisfactory")))

levels(eis$epa_impact)
```

Our data also has several date columns. When you subtract one date from another, R gives you the number of days in between. We'll use that to make two new numeric columns: `comment_days`, the number of days the public had to comment on the statement, and `epa_lag`, the number of days it took the EPA to send its comment letter after the statement was filed:

```{r clean-days, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis %>%
  mutate(comment_days = as.numeric(comment_due_date - federal_register_date),
         epa_lag = as.numeric(comment_letter_date - filed_date))
```

Last, let's add the region of the country each filing is in. R comes with a few built-in vectors about U.S. states, including `state.abb` (the two-letter abbreviations) and `state.region` (the census region). We can put them together into a little lookup table and join it on, just like we did in week 5:

```{r clean-region, purl=FALSE}
state_regions <- tibble(state = state.abb, region = as.character(state.region))

eis <- eis %>%
  left_join(state_regions, by = "state")

table(eis$region, useNA = "ifany")
```

Filings without a state, or with a code that isn't one of the 50 states (like `PR` or `DC`), get an `NA` region.

### Checking our new variables

It's a good idea to look at a new variable before you trust it. Let's check `comment_days`:

```{r check-comment, purl=FALSE}
summary(eis$comment_days)
hist(eis$comment_days)
```

Some of these comment periods are negative, and one is more than five years long! These are probably data entry errors. Everything is crammed into one bar, because the bins have to stretch all the way from the smallest value to the largest. We'll treat anything below 0 or longer than a year as missing, and do the same for `epa_lag`:

```{r clean-errors, purl=FALSE}
eis <- eis %>%
  mutate(comment_days = if_else(comment_days >= 0 & comment_days <= 365, comment_days, NA),
         epa_lag = if_else(epa_lag >= 0 & epa_lag <= 365, epa_lag, NA))
```

Now let's try that histogram again, with one bin per day:

```{r check-comment-again, purl=FALSE}
hist(eis$comment_days, breaks = 0:365)
```

Much better. Most of the comment periods are bunched up at a couple of specific lengths. We'll figure out why in a bit.

## Plotting with **`ggplot2`**

**`ggplot2`** is a plotting package that makes it simple to create complex plots
from data in a data frame. It provides a more programmatic interface for
specifying what variables to plot, how they are displayed, and general visual
properties. Therefore, we only need minimal changes if the underlying data change
or if we decide to change from a bar plot to a scatterplot. This helps in creating
publication quality plots with minimal amounts of adjustments and tweaking.

**`ggplot2`** functions like data in the 'long' format, i.e., a column for every dimension,
and a row for every observation. Well-structured data will save you lots of time
when making figures with **`ggplot2`**

ggplot graphics are built step by step by adding new elements. Adding layers in
this fashion allows for extensive flexibility and customization of plots.

To build a ggplot, we will use the following basic template that can be used for different types of plots:

```
ggplot(data = <DATA>, mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>)) +  <GEOM_FUNCTION>()
```

- use the `ggplot()` function and bind the plot to a specific data frame using the
      `data` argument

```{r, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis)
```

- define a mapping (using the aesthetic (`aes`) function), by selecting the variables to be plotted and specifying how to present them in the graph, e.g. as x/y positions or characteristics such as size, shape, color, etc.

```{r, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = comment_days))
```

- add 'geoms' – graphical representations of the data in the plot (points,
  lines, bars). **`ggplot2`** offers many different geoms; we will use some
  common ones today, including:

      * `geom_histogram()` for histograms
      * `geom_bar()` for bar charts
      * `geom_point()` for scatter plots, dot plots, etc.
      * `geom_boxplot()` for, well, boxplots!
      * `geom_line()` for trend lines, time series, etc.

To add a geom to the plot use the `+` operator. Because we have one continuous variable,
let's use `geom_histogram()` first:

```{r first-ggplot, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = comment_days)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

ggplot picked 30 bins for us, and gave us a message about it. Like with `hist()`, we can choose the bins ourselves. The `binwidth` argument sets how wide each bin is, so `binwidth = 1` gives us one bar per day. Let's also zoom in on the first 120 days with `xlim()`:

```{r ggplot-binwidth, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = comment_days)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  xlim(0, 120)
```

ggplot warns us that it removed some rows. Those are the `NA` values, plus anything longer than 120 days. Notice the two big spikes, one at 31 days and one at 45 days. Keep those in mind.

The `+` in the **`ggplot2`** package is particularly useful because it allows you
to modify existing `ggplot` objects. This means you can easily set up plot
templates and conveniently explore different types of plots, so the above
plot can also be generated with code like this:

```{r, first-ggplot-with-plus, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
# Assign plot to a variable
eis_plot <- ggplot(data = eis,
                   mapping = aes(x = comment_days))

# Draw the plot
eis_plot +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)
```

**Notes**

- Anything you put in the `ggplot()` function can be seen by any geom layers
  that you add (i.e., these are universal plot settings). This includes the x- and
  y-axis mapping you set up in `aes()`.
- You can also specify mappings for a given geom independently of the
  mappings defined globally in the `ggplot()` function.
- The `+` sign used to add new layers must be placed at the end of the line containing
the *previous* layer. If, instead, the `+` sign is added at the beginning of the line
containing the new layer, **`ggplot2`** will not add the new layer and will return an
error message.

```{r, ggplot-with-plus-position, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
# This is the correct syntax for adding layers
eis_plot +
  geom_histogram()

# This will not add the new layer and will return an error message
eis_plot
  + geom_histogram()
```

## Building your plots iteratively

Building plots with **`ggplot2`** is typically an iterative process. We start by
defining the dataset we'll use, lay out the axes, and choose a geom. Let's count up the filings for each agency with `geom_bar()`:

```{r create-ggplot-object, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = agency)) +
    geom_bar()
```

Then, we start modifying this plot to extract more information from it. For
instance, the agency names are so long that they run into each other. We can fix that by putting `agency` on the y-axis instead:

```{r flip-axis, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(y = agency)) +
    geom_bar()
```

We can also add colors for all the bars. For bars, `fill` sets the color inside the bar, and `color` sets the color of the outline:

```{r adding-colors, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(y = agency)) +
    geom_bar(fill = "darkgreen")
```

Or to color each stage in the plot differently, you could use a vector as an input to the argument **fill**. **`ggplot2`** will provide a different color corresponding to different values in the vector. Here is an example where we fill with **`stage`**:

```{r fill-by-stage, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(y = agency)) +
    geom_bar(aes(fill = stage))
```

We can also specify the colors directly inside the mapping provided in the `ggplot()` function. This will be seen by all geom layers and the mapping will be determined by the x- and y-axis set up in `aes()`.

```{r fill-by-stage2, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(y = agency, fill = stage)) +
    geom_bar()
```

Notice that we can change the geom layer and colors will be still determined by **`stage`**. For example, we can tell `geom_bar()` to put the bars for each stage side by side instead of stacking them:

```{r dodge, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(y = agency, fill = stage)) +
    geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

## Counting with `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()`

`geom_bar()` counts the rows in each group for us, so we only have to give it one variable. Let's try it with a couple of other columns. Here's the EPA's impact rating:

```{r bar-impact, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact)) +
    geom_bar()
```

The ratings show up in the order we set when we made `epa_impact` a factor, not alphabetically. There's that big `NA` bar again. We can fill by stage to see what kind of filings got rated:

```{r bar-impact-stage, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact, fill = stage)) +
    geom_bar()
```

And here's the number of filings in each region:

```{r bar-region, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = region)) +
    geom_bar()
```

Sometimes we've already counted things ourselves, like with `count()`. In that case we use `geom_col()` instead, and give it the counts as one of the variables:

```{r state-counts, purl=FALSE}
state_counts <- eis %>%
  filter(!is.na(region)) %>%
  count(state, region)
```

There are 50 states, so we'll put them on the y-axis like we did with the agencies:

```{r state-col, fig.height=8, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = state_counts, mapping = aes(x = n, y = state, fill = region)) +
    geom_col()
```

California has the most filings by far, and the western states in general have a lot more than the rest of the country.

Use `ggplot()` to create a scatter plot of `epa_lag` and

```{r scatter-challenge, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = eis, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact, y = epa_lag)) +

```

## Boxplot

We can use boxplots to visualize the distribution of `epa_lag` within each impact rating. We'll stick to the draft statements that the EPA actually rated:

```{r drafts-rated, purl=FALSE}
drafts_rated <- eis %>%
  filter(stage == "Draft", !is.na(epa_impact), !is.na(epa_lag))
```

```{r boxplot, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = drafts_rated, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact, y = epa_lag)) +
    geom_boxplot()
```

The worse the rating, the longer the EPA tends to take to send its comment letter.

By adding points to boxplot, we can have a better idea of the number of
measurements and of their distribution.

Let's also use the geometry "jitter". `geom_jitter` is almost like `geom_point` but it allows you to visualize the density of points because it adds a small amount of random variation to the location of each point.

```{r boxplot-with-points, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = drafts_rated, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact, y = epa_lag)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0) +
    geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, color = "tomato") #notice our color needs to be in quotations
```

Notice how the boxplot layer is behind the jitter layer? What do you need to
change in the code to put the boxplot in front of the points such that it's not
hidden?

<div class = "blue">

### Challenges

1. Boxplots are useful summaries, but hide the *shape* of the distribution. For
example, if the distribution is bimodal, we would not see it in a
boxplot. An alternative to the boxplot is the violin plot, where the shape
(of the density of points) is drawn.

- Replace the box plot code from above with a violin plot; see `geom_violin()`.

2. In many types of data, it is important to consider the *scale* of the
observations.  For example, it may be worth changing the scale of the axis to
better distribute the observations in the space of the plot.  Changing the scale
of the axes is done similarly to adding/modifying other components (i.e., by
incrementally adding commands). Try making these modifications:

- Use the violin plot you made in Q1 and adjust `epa_lag` to be on the log~10~ scale; see `scale_y_log10()`.

3. Make a new plot to explore the distribution of `comment_days` just for the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management using `geom_boxplot()`. Overlay a jitter/scatter plot of the comment periods of the two agencies behind the boxplots. Then, add an `aes()` argument to color the datapoints (but not the boxplots) according to the stage of the filing. Leave out the "Other" stage.

*Hint:* Remember the two spikes in our histogram of `comment_days`, at 31 and 45 days? Does coloring by stage help explain them?

<details>
<summary>ANSWER</summary>
```{r boxplot-challenges, fig.width=10, purl=FALSE}
#1 + 2

ggplot(data = drafts_rated, mapping = aes(x = epa_impact, y = epa_lag)) +
    geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, color = "tomato") +
    geom_violin(alpha = 0) +
    scale_y_log10()

#3
eis %>%
  filter(agency == "Forest Service" | agency == "Bureau of Land Management", stage != "Other") %>%
 ggplot(mapping = aes(x = agency, y = comment_days)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, aes(color = stage)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0)
```

R warns about infinite values in #2 because a few filings have an `epa_lag` of 0 days, and the log of 0 is negative infinity.

In #3, the final statements pile up at around 30 days and the drafts at 45 days or more. The two spikes in the histogram are mostly the two stages.

</details>
</div>
<br>

## Plotting time series data

Let's calculate number of filings per year for each agency. First we need
to group the data and count records within each group. We can quickly use the dplyr function `count` to do this. `count` is very similar to the function `tally` we have seen before, but it internally calls `group_by` before the function and `ungroup` after.

```{r, purl=FALSE}
yearly_counts <- eis %>%
                 count(filed_year, agency)
```

Time series data can be visualized as a line plot with years on the x axis and counts
on the y axis:

```{r first-time-series, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = yearly_counts, mapping = aes(x = filed_year, y = n)) +
     geom_line()
```

Unfortunately, this does not work because we plotted data for all the agencies
together. We need to tell ggplot to draw a line for each agency by modifying
the aesthetic function to include `group = agency`:

```{r time-series-by-agency, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = yearly_counts, mapping = aes(x = filed_year, y = n, group = agency)) +
    geom_line()
```

We will be able to distinguish agencies in the plot if we add colors (using `color` also automatically groups the data):

```{r time-series-with-colors, purl=FALSE}
ggplot(data = yearly_counts, mapping = aes(x = filed_year, y = n, color = agency)) +
    geom_line()
```
